fr:title.text: How to Specify a Large Language Model?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: How to Specify a Large Language Model?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Consider the (perhaps extreme) problem of specifying the "correct" behavior of a large language model like Chat GPT. The technologists who have built these LLMs are probably more aware than anyone—no one really knows what the correct behavior of an artificial intelligence is or should be. We want it to be helpful, knowledgeable, and honest—yes, but there are also some things we would rather it not produce even though it could do so in principle within the bounds of being helpful, knowledgeable, and honest. These things include somewhat-universally-agreed-upon things like child porn and slanderous and libelous deep fakes. In more of a grey area, they can also include politically inconvenient facts or references to certain events in history about which we remain sensitive.

In other words, we want the LLM to be kind, or to have a value system of some kind. An LLM should not encourage someone to kill themselves. It shouldn't help someone build a bomb. It shouldn't help someone plan to commit a crime (although .. maybe it should help a revolutionary overthrow a tyrant?). The problem with asking an LLM to behave ethically is who is to say what is right, and good, and true? What value system should dominate? People will have different philosophies on what they think the behavior of an LLM should be, but we are far from any point of consensus on what that should be. Yes, most of us want an LLM to align with what is good, virtuous, and true; the problem is that it is hard to know what is good, virtuous, and true, and thus hard to train an AI to align itself with that. (Think of the film I, Robot as a meditation on the unintended—and disasterous, tyranical—consequences of instilling a seemingly straightforward and simple value system into an intelligent robot.)

I would argue that the problem of correctly specifying an LLM is the problem that religion tends to address—one of value, meaning, and knowing goodness. This is an ancient problem, one that I would argue is so nuanced and complex that it can barely be told in story form, much less in prose, and even less a formal specification.

fr:title.text: The Computer Scientist's Approach to Proposition and Proof (About Software)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Computer Scientist's Approach to Proposition and Proof (About Software)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Some software is straightforward to specify because it strongly resembles the rigorous and well-defined world of mathematics. For example, chip design or software implementing zero-knowledge proofs will be relatively straightforward to specify correctly because the purpose of the software is expressly mathematical, or clearly derived from within a formal system. In these cases, the specification tends to be abundantly clear because the work of settling on the correct definition and desired behavior of things was solved mathematically before it was translated into software.

However, software does much more than mathematical computation. As it gets higher in abstraction, software can become a social and financial intermediary between people or even an agent of its own. Software runs human-computer interfaces, the flow of a sales team's CRM, and the media by which news gets reported and propagated. Software makes music, tells stories, implements art and design. It manages money and communication between people. In these cases, the intended behavior of software doesn't always have a clear and definable formal specification couched in mathematical terms. Instead, at these higher layers of abstraction, software can become difficult to specify—or describe in a formal language—correctly.

The specification of LLMs may be intractable, but I think we can make progress in something less, say, human: smart contracts. What we will find is that smart contracts lie at a rich intersection between low-level, technical properties and high-level, more "human" properties. Can we reasonably specify smart contracts in a rigorous and correct way? How can we strengthen their specifications to be more clear, accurate, and useful?
Smart contracts can have deceptively difficult specifications.

Dexter2 is an AMM on the Tezos blockchain that has been formally verified by at least three different groups using three different formal verification tools. Each was based on the same informal specification. The informal specification describes the contract interface, including its entrypoint functions, error messages, outgoing transactions, the contents of its storage, some invariants of the storage (including that its store of tokens never fully depletes), fees, and the logic of each of the entrypoint functions. This is a standard and detailed contract specification.

However, while the specification is detailed on the contract design and interface, it doesn’t include anything about expected or desired behavior from an economic perspective. This is not because the expected or desired economic behavior is unknown or uninteresting. It was clearly articulated by Vitalik Buterin, co-founder of Ethereum, in what he wrote in March 2018 about AMMs on the online forum Ethereum Research. Buterin proposed that AMMs trade between a pair of tokens along an indifference curve:

where x represents the quantity held by the contract of the token being traded in, y represents the quantity held by the contract of the token being traded out, and k is a constant. The tokens held by the contract come from liquidity providers, which are investors who deposit tokens into the AMM in exchange for a reward, most often a share of transaction fees. That k is constant means that a trade of \Delta x of one token yields \Delta y of another such that the product from above stays constant at k:

Buterin argued that an AMM that trades along this indifference curve features efficient price discovery. He also argued that it can properly incentivize liquidity providers by charging a 0.3% fee on each trade to give to them.

We can probably convince ourselves that the informal specification of Dexter2 features these economic qualities described by Buterin, including efficient price discovery and some suitable incentive mechanism so that investors deposit tokens into the AMM contract and provide liquidity to the market; however, concluding that the informal specification or its formal counterparts actually imply any of these economic behaviors is not a given fact. AMM fees and liquidity provision alone are highly complex topics, and are the subject of several economic studies, including on choosing optimal transaction fees, how liquidity providers react to market changes, and how all of that relates to the curvature of the indifference curve xy= k. It was also shown that front-running attacks can warp the incentive scheme of the blockchain itself in such a way that could compromise its underlying security.

There is then an outstanding question of whether any of Dexter2’s specifications are correct with regards to the desired—indeed, essential—high-level economic and game-theoretic behavior of the resulting AMM. Not only do these important economic and game-theoretic factors not make it into any of Dexter2’s specifications, formal or informal, but to complicate matters a brief study of the three formalizations of Dexter2’s informal specification reveals that each differs substantively both in how the properties of the informal specification are formalized, and in what assumptions are made in the process of verification.

Furthermore, were we to try to formally specify some of the aforementioned high-level economic and game-theoretic behaviors on the Dexter2 contract it is not at all obvious how we would go about doing so. Most specification languages and models of computation are too low-level to easily admit clear specifications of such properties. What model or framework would we use, for example, to specify that Dexter2 facilitate an efficient market?

As codebases go, Dexter2 is quite small—only a few thousand lines—but as we’ve seen much is expected of it in terms of its economic and game-theoretic behavior; because AMMs like Dexter2 routinely manage billions of USD worth of funds, much is also at risk in case of a bug. Furthermore, despite the fact that they are not present in any of Dexter2’s specifications, it is difficult to conceptualize a notion of Dexter2’s correctness that does not include some of the economic properties that we have just mentioned, directly or indirectly. It is, however, not obvious that these properties hold by reading any of the aforementioned specifications.

The problem that Dexter2 illustrates is that smart contracts have social, game theoretic, and crypto-economic properties that are difficult to state in a prose specification, much less in a formal way. This in contrast with something like ZK circuits, which are an interesting, contrasting case: a hash function's specification is an equation, so fixing an interface in Lean is enough to make optimisation safe — a discipline that would have bought nothing here.

fr:title.text: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities Due to Poor Specification

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities Due to Poor Specification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Smart contracts are vulnerable due to incorrect code, but equally due to incorrect specification (or design). There are more examples of this that can possibly be included here, but I have written up a few examples. We would recognize each of these exploits as attacks, despite the fact that the contracts were functioning as specified, which tells us that the specifications were erroneous as they did not accurately capture the intended economic behaviors. To the contrary, they permitted unintended and pathological behavior.

Beanstalk is (was) an Ethereum-based stablecoin protocol which uses a decentralized governance protocol. This governance protocol features an emergency commit function, which gives a supermajority of governance votes power to quickly respond to an emergency by approving and executing a proposal in one single vote. The goal of said emergency commit function is to allow governance to respond quickly to an emergency, providing added security in the face of unforeseen vulnerabilities.

In a turn of grim irony, this very emergency response mechanism turned out to be the source of a catastrophic exploit. On April 17, 2022, an attacker used a flash loan to temporarily buy a supermajority of governance tokens and execute a proposal, draining the contract of approximately 77 million USD in lost contract assets A flash loan is a loan mediated by a smart contract and issued for the duration of a single, atomic transaction. Due to its atomicity, a flash loan removes the creditor’s risk of debt default, and thus enables enormous, uncollateralized loans. For example, the Aave flash loan pool has had in excess of 1 billion USD which can be loaned out. Flash loans can introduce unintuitive contract behavior, deviating from that of traditional markets. Importantly, the Beanstalk attack leveraged the unexpected behavior due to the availability of flash loans, exploiting the faulty design of the governance mechanism rather than incorrect code.

fr:title.text: Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny Hack (2021)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny Hack (2021)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: More examples of successful flash loan attacks include attacks on the Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny, two DeFi contracts on the Binance Smart Chain (BSC). Attackers used flash loans to make huge trades and temporarily manipulate market prices of certain assets. Both of these contracts used these market prices in the contract logic, and in both cases this lead to pathological—though, again, correct according to the flawed specification—contract behavior. In May 2021, an attacker drained the Spartan Protocol contract for a profit of roughly the equivalent of 30 million USD. Another attacker drained Pancake Bunny of 114k WBNB and 697k BUNNY tokens, amounting to about 45 million USD at the time in lost funds.

Finally, Mango Markets, a Solana-based DEX, was attacked in October 2022 for approximately 116 million USD in contract assets. The attack consisted of a complicated and subtle trading strategy which only a sophisticated trader would be able to see and exploit. CoinDesk reported that the attacker did everything within the parameters of the platform’s design. Avraham Eisenberg, the attacker, wrote:

html:p.html:em: "I believe all of our actions were legal open market actions, using the protocol as designed, even if the development team did not fully anticipate all the consequences of setting parameters the way they are."

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Nomad is (was) a cross-chain bridge protocol. In August 2022, more than 500 hacker addresses exploited a bug introduced by a faulty upgrade to one of the Nomad smart contracts. The upgrade incorrectly added the null address (0x000...000) as a trusted root, which turned off a key safety check, allowing anyone to withdraw arbitrary amounts of funds from the Nomad contract to their wallet by calling the contract with a particular payload. The attack resulted in 190 million USD in lost funds.

Similarly, Uranium Finance, an AMM, suffered a costly exploit after a faulty contract upgrade. The original contract contained a constant, k, equal to 1_000 in three different places, which was used to price trades. The update changed this value to 10_000 in two places but not the third, presumably to calculate trades with higher precision. The result of this was that the attacker could swap virtually nothing in for 98% of the total balance of any output token, which resulted in a loss of 50 million USD of contract funds. NowSwap, a nearly identical application, upgraded with the same error and incurred a loss of 1 million USD.

Incorrect software specifications are a problem because they can invalidate the security guarantees offered by formal verification, offer a false sense of security, misguide developers, and most importantly open code up to vulnerabilities. Indeed, for smart contracts, poor specifications are a common source of catastrophic vulnerabilities and losses of funds.

Considering this, what is the role of formal proposition and proof (formal verification), especially in proof assistants, applied to software vulnerabilities? How do we address the issue of incorrect specification?
